items.title: Ron Carter interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 17, 1999
items.q: Highlights include his tenure with Miles Davis from 1963-68... We’d been off about four months, and he told us this is a benefit... I was the spokesperson of the band

ctx.x: That was done at Lincoln Center. People don’t realize that Miles was a real civil activist and he would often play for these civil rights fundraisers. And that night was a fundraiser for some civil rights group, I can’t remember, NAACP or something like that. We’d been off about four months, and he told us this is a benefit. So maybe I guess I was the spokesperson of the band said, it’s a benefit, okay, well why don’t you benefit them and let us have our money? And if I decide I want to benefit them I’ll give…
recorded. We didn’t know it was recorded until a year after the record was out, so that was a whole other process, a whole other thing on the scene. And that’s one of the stories behind that record.

items.title: Ron Carter — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: That came during the course of my time with Miles. ... I'd been in the Miles band

ctx.x: Yeah. He was honest, he was blunt, you know. While it wasn't a new feeling to have .. to hear this, it was kind of a drag because you'd put all this time in in this industry, call it orchestra playing, and to hear that one of the items on the hiring peoples' list is what race you are, it just seems to be what a waste of effort and energy on their part. It seems to me that music sounds great when great players play them. Whatever color they are. But when you are eighteen, you don't think that philosophically; you…
